doc_name: IVF patient guide (adapted from UW Medicine, 2025)
content: IVF happens in a set order: ovarian stimulation with injectable medicines, monitoring, the trigger shot to mature the eggs, egg retrieval, sperm collection, fertilization in the lab, assisted hatching when needed, embryo transfer, and care after the transfer. Your doctor will go through each step and the specific medicines with you before you start.

doc_name: IVF patient guide (adapted from UW Medicine, 2025)
content: In stimulation, injectable fertility medicines help several follicles (the small fluid sacs that hold eggs) grow and mature at the same time, instead of the usual one. The injections go either under the skin (subcutaneous) or into a muscle (intramuscular). Your doctor reviews exactly which medicines you will use and how to give them.

doc_name: IVF patient guide (adapted from UW Medicine, 2025)
content: During stimulation you may come in as often as every day. Each monitoring visit usually means a blood draw to check hormone levels and a transvaginal ultrasound to measure how the follicles are growing. The team stays in close contact with you after stimulation ends too.

doc_name: IVF patient guide (adapted from UW Medicine, 2025)
section: When a cycle is stopped or cancelled
content: Sometimes stimulation has to stop. If the ovaries respond too little, the team will talk with you about other treatment options. If they respond too strongly, there is a risk of ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS), and the cycle is cancelled to keep you safe. Rarely, the egg retrieval itself is cancelled shortly before, for example if ovulation happens too early or hormone levels drop.

doc_name: IVF patient guide (adapted from UW Medicine, 2025)
section: Trigger shot and timing of egg retrieval
content: When your doctor tells you the follicles are ready, you give yourself the ovulation trigger injection (the trigger shot). Egg retrieval is then scheduled 34 to 36 hours after the trigger, so the timing of that injection is very important. Follow the exact time your clinic gives you.

doc_name: IVF patient guide (adapted from UW Medicine, 2025)
content: Egg retrieval is an outpatient procedure, so you go home the same day. You receive deep sedation through an IV in your arm. Guided by a transvaginal ultrasound, the doctor passes a thin needle through the vaginal wall into each ovary and draws fluid out of as many follicles as possible. An embryologist then looks through the fluid to find the eggs.

doc_name: IVF patient guide (adapted from UW Medicine, 2025)
content: Problems from sedation are rare. One rare risk is short-term or permanent nerve injury from how the body is positioned. To lower this, your legs are placed in position while you are still awake, and the anesthesia team watches you closely the whole time. If anesthesia is not right for you, the team can use other medicines.

doc_name: IVF patient guide (adapted from UW Medicine, 2025)
section: Recovery after egg retrieval: does it hurt?
content: Mild to moderate pelvic or belly pain after retrieval is common and usually settles within 1 to 2 days. Over-the-counter pain relievers usually help. Rarely, the needle can injure nearby organs such as the bladder, bowel or blood vessels; in rare cases this needs emergency surgery and sometimes a blood transfusion. Pelvic infection after retrieval is uncommon, and is more likely if you have had a pelvic infection before or have endometriosis on the ovary.

doc_name: IVF patient guide (adapted from UW Medicine, 2025)
content: Eggs can be frozen to use in IVF later. People freeze eggs before cancer treatment, because of a chronic illness, or to delay having children. Not every frozen egg survives thawing, and some thawed eggs do not fertilize, so egg freezing is not a guarantee of a future pregnancy.

doc_name: IVF patient guide (adapted from UW Medicine, 2025)
content: A partner's sperm sample is collected on the day of egg retrieval. Donor sperm is thawed that same day. If a partner may not be able to give a sample on the day, sperm can be collected and frozen ahead of time as a backup. It is rare for sperm not to survive thawing.

doc_name: IVF patient guide (adapted from UW Medicine, 2025)
content: There are two ways to fertilize eggs in the lab. In standard insemination, sperm are placed in a dish with the eggs and enter them on their own. In ICSI (intracytoplasmic sperm injection), an embryologist injects one sperm into each egg; it is more complex, costs more, and is used when the chance with standard insemination looks low. The team chooses based on your diagnosis, past treatment results, and the number and quality of eggs and sperm.

doc_name: IVF patient guide (adapted from UW Medicine, 2025)
content: Assisted hatching uses a laser to make a small opening in the embryo's outer shell. It is done when a few cells need to be taken from the embryo (a biopsy) for preimplantation genetic testing, which can check for a specific disease or for the right number of chromosomes.

doc_name: IVF patient guide (adapted from UW Medicine, 2025)
content: In a fresh transfer, embryos are placed into the uterus 3 or 5 days after egg retrieval, using a thin catheter passed through the cervix. Before your cycle, the team may suggest a mock (practice) transfer with a soft catheter to spot any problems in advance. You may feel mild cramping when the catheter goes in or have slight spotting afterward.

doc_name: IVF patient guide (adapted from UW Medicine, 2025)
content: The number of embryos transferred depends on your age, embryo quality and other medical factors. The aim is the best chance of pregnancy with the lowest chance of twins or triplets, so the team transfers the smallest number that still gives a good chance.

doc_name: IVF patient guide (adapted from UW Medicine, 2025)
content: After the transfer, progesterone helps the embryo implant. It is given as an injection into the muscle or placed in the vagina. After a fresh transfer it is usually continued until about the 8th week of pregnancy. Never stop or change progesterone on your own; ask your care team first.

doc_name: IVF patient guide (adapted from UW Medicine, 2025)
content: Good-quality extra embryos can be frozen for future attempts at building your family. Embryos that reach the blastocyst stage, 5 to 7 days old, are the ones frozen. What happens to embryos you do not use is decided in advance, together with your partner if you have one, in the IVF consent form.

doc_name: IVF patient guide (adapted from UW Medicine, 2025)
content: Common side effects of IVF medicines include mild bruising or soreness where you inject, temporary redness or itching of the skin, nausea and sometimes vomiting, breast tenderness, more vaginal discharge, mood swings and tiredness.

doc_name: IVF patient guide (adapted from UW Medicine, 2025)
content: Mild OHSS can cause nausea, bloating and pelvic discomfort, and usually gets better within a few days after egg collection. Severe OHSS can enlarge the ovaries and cause fluid to build up in the belly and sometimes the lungs. Warning signs are dehydration, trouble breathing and severe belly pain; contact your care team right away if you notice them. Very rarely (under 1% of cases) OHSS leads to blood clots or kidney failure.

doc_name: IVF patient guide (adapted from UW Medicine, 2025)
content: An ectopic pregnancy grows outside the uterus; with IVF the risk is about 1%. Call your clinic straight away if you have sharp, stabbing pain, vaginal bleeding, dizziness, fainting or lower back pain. A heterotopic pregnancy (one in the uterus and one in a tube) also has about a 1% risk; it usually needs surgery to remove the tubal pregnancy, and the pregnancy in the uterus can often continue.

doc_name: IVF patient guide (adapted from UW Medicine, 2025)
content: IVF makes twins or triplets more likely, especially when more embryos are transferred. Multiple pregnancies carry more risk of early labor and premature birth, heavy bleeding, cesarean delivery, high blood pressure in pregnancy and gestational diabetes. This is why transferring the fewest embryos needed is recommended.

doc_name: IVF patient guide (adapted from UW Medicine, 2025)
content: The chance of miscarriage after IVF is similar to a natural pregnancy and rises with age: about 15% for women in their 20s and more than 50% for women in their 40s.

doc_name: IVF patient guide (adapted from UW Medicine, 2025)
section: Birth defects, genetic risks and ovarian cancer
content: Birth defects affect 2% to 3% of all babies. The rate is slightly higher with fertility problems, mostly because of older age and the cause of infertility. It is not clear that IVF itself raises the risk; it may be slightly higher with ICSI. There is a small increase in rare imprinting disorders. Older studies suggested fertility medicines might be linked to ovarian cancer, but newer, higher-quality studies show no clear link.

doc_name: IVF patient guide (adapted from UW Medicine, 2025)
content: IVF can lead to a pregnancy and can leave you with frozen embryos for later, but no step is guaranteed to work. IVF may not result in a pregnancy or a live birth, and a pregnancy may not end in a healthy full-term delivery. You decide, with your doctor, whether the benefits are worth the risks for you.

doc_name: Fertility evaluation guide (adapted from ASRM Committee Opinion, 2026)
section: When to see a fertility doctor for an evaluation
content: If you have regular unprotected sex with a male partner and no known fertility problem, an evaluation is recommended after 12 months of trying if you are under 35, and after 6 months if you are 35 or older. Over 40, it often makes sense to start sooner. Evaluation can start right away if there is a known reason, such as irregular cycles.

doc_name: Fertility evaluation guide (adapted from ASRM Committee Opinion, 2026)
section: Reasons to be evaluated right away
content: Start the evaluation without waiting if you have cycles shorter than 25 or longer than 35 days, bleeding between periods or no periods, repeated pregnancy losses, known or suspected problems with the uterus or tubes or endometriosis, a partner with possible sperm problems, sexual difficulties, past chemotherapy or radiation, or if you are planning egg freezing or using donor eggs or sperm.

doc_name: Fertility evaluation guide (adapted from ASRM Committee Opinion, 2026)
section: LGBTQ+ patients, single women and donor sperm
content: Infertility is not only about a year of trying with a male partner. Single women, same-sex female couples and others using donor sperm get a targeted evaluation instead of having to 'try' first, and transgender and nonbinary patients get an evaluation tailored to them. Reciprocal IVF is an option for same-sex couples. Relationship status or sexual orientation should never be used to deny or delay care.

doc_name: Fertility evaluation guide (adapted from ASRM Committee Opinion, 2026)
content: When a male partner is involved, both partners are evaluated at the same time. A semen analysis should be done at the start, because sperm-related factors play a part in up to 40% of cases.

doc_name: Fertility evaluation guide (adapted from ASRM Committee Opinion, 2026)
content: The core evaluation checks four things: whether you ovulate, the shape of the uterus, whether the fallopian tubes are open, and, with a male partner, a semen analysis. The doctor also takes a detailed history of your cycles, pregnancies, health, medicines, family and lifestyle. A routine pelvic exam is usually not needed if you have a pelvic ultrasound.

doc_name: Fertility evaluation guide (adapted from ASRM Committee Opinion, 2026)
content: Problems with ovulation cause about 40% of infertility in women. Common causes include PCOS (now also called PMOS), weight changes, very intense exercise, thyroid problems and high prolactin. If your cycles are regular, every 25 to 35 days, and you have no excess hair growth, you are very likely ovulating and usually do not need tests to confirm it. Irregular or missing periods are enough to show an ovulation problem.

doc_name: Fertility evaluation guide (adapted from ASRM Committee Opinion, 2026)
section: Ovulation tests: progesterone, LH kits, temperature charts
content: A progesterone blood test about a week before your expected period can confirm you ovulated. Home LH (ovulation) kits detect the hormone surge 1 to 2 days before ovulation, but can give false positives with PCOS. Basal body temperature charting is not recommended because it is unreliable and cannot tell you when to time sex.

doc_name: Fertility evaluation guide (adapted from ASRM Committee Opinion, 2026)
content: If your cycles are irregular and your FSH and estradiol levels are normal, the next step is usually an evaluation for PCOS (PMOS). If there are signs of high androgens, such as excess hair growth or acne, your doctor may also screen for a related adrenal condition. AMH can be part of the picture for PCOS, but there is no single cutoff.

doc_name: Fertility evaluation guide (adapted from ASRM Committee Opinion, 2026)
section: Ovarian reserve: AMH, antral follicle count, FSH
content: Ovarian reserve tests estimate how many eggs you have. They include AMH (a blood test you can take on any day of your cycle), FSH and estradiol on cycle days 2 to 4, and an ultrasound count of small follicles (antral follicle count). Their main use is to predict how your ovaries will respond to stimulation and to plan treatment. Age is still the strongest predictor of fertility.

doc_name: Fertility evaluation guide (adapted from ASRM Committee Opinion, 2026)
section: What AMH does and doesn't tell you
content: AMH reflects the number of eggs, not their quality. On its own, it is poor at predicting whether you can get pregnant naturally, and a low AMH should not be used to exclude anyone from treatment. AMH can vary within a cycle, so repeated testing is not recommended; one result, read together with your age and history, is the standard. Your doctor will explain what your own result means.

doc_name: Fertility evaluation guide (adapted from ASRM Committee Opinion, 2026)
section: Checking the uterus: ultrasound, SHG, HSG, hysteroscopy
content: About 16% of people having a fertility evaluation have something in the uterus, most often polyps, less often fibroids or scar tissue. A transvaginal ultrasound is the best first test. A saline ultrasound (sonohysterography) is very accurate for finding problems inside the uterus. An HSG X-ray shows the shape of the cavity but misses about half of polyps and fibroids. Hysteroscopy, a camera in the uterus, can both diagnose and treat.

doc_name: Fertility evaluation guide (adapted from ASRM Committee Opinion, 2026)
section: Checking the fallopian tubes: HSG and HyCoSy
content: Blocked or damaged tubes need to be ruled out. The most common test is an HSG, an X-ray with dye; a newer option is HyCoSy, an ultrasound with contrast, and both are similarly accurate. If one tube looks blocked near the uterus, there is more than a 40% chance it is actually open on later testing, so results sometimes need a second test. Laparoscopy (keyhole surgery) is not used routinely just to check the tubes.

doc_name: Fertility evaluation guide (adapted from ASRM Committee Opinion, 2026)
content: Endometriosis and scar tissue can affect fertility. An ultrasound can find some signs, such as an endometrioma (a cyst on the ovary). Laparoscopy is the only way to diagnose endometriosis directly, but it is not done routinely; it is reserved for people with signs of pelvic disease or another reason for surgery, such as very painful periods.

doc_name: Fertility evaluation guide (adapted from ASRM Committee Opinion, 2026)
section: Tests that are usually not needed
content: Many tests are not routinely recommended unless there is a specific reason: postcoital tests, endometrial biopsy, routine thyroid (TSH) or prolactin tests without symptoms, clotting (thrombophilia) and immune tests, chromosome tests (karyotype), advanced sperm function tests, and laparoscopy for unexplained infertility. Your doctor will order a test when it would change your care.

doc_name: Fertility evaluation guide (adapted from ASRM Committee Opinion, 2026)
content: Cervical mucus is a useful sign: on days with clear, stretchy 'egg-white' mucus, the chance of conceiving is about 40% per day, compared with 1% to 6% on other days. Watching mucus changes predicts the fertile window better than timing sex to ovulation alone.
